nameStory: The name 'juvenilis' comes from Latin meaning 'youthful' or 'young,' though scientists aren't entirely sure why this particular spider earned this designation. It might refer to the species being relatively recently discovered compared to its relatives, or perhaps early specimens collected were juveniles that confused researchers about the adult size.
description: Coras juvenilis is a funnel weaver spider that belongs to a group known for creating distinctive sheet webs with funnel-shaped retreats. Like other funnel weavers, it has a brownish, elongated body with relatively long legs that help it dart quickly across its web to catch prey. These are medium-sized spiders that are quite rare in New England, with very few confirmed sightings in the region.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates a horizontal sheet web with a distinctive funnel-shaped retreat at one corner where the spider hides, waiting to feel vibrations from trapped insects

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened body with a brownish coloration and relatively long, sturdy legs built for quick movement across web surfaces

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely fast runner that darts out from its funnel retreat when prey hits the web, then quickly retreats back to safety

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two rows, giving the spider good vision for detecting movement both on the web and in the surrounding area

habitat: Found in forested areas where they can anchor their sheet webs between fallen logs, rock crevices, or low vegetation. They prefer spots with some moisture retention but good air circulation, often in areas with mixed deciduous and coniferous trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish territory and construct their characteristic funnel webs in suitable locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily observed. Mating occurs during this time with females guarding egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be active in early fall, but begin preparing for winter dormancy as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter in protected locations like under bark or in rock crevices, becoming inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Coras juvenilis is so rare in New England that it has been confirmed only once in the entire region, making any sighting a truly exceptional discovery that could contribute valuable data to our understanding of spider distribution!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other funnel weaver species in the Coras genus, but the funnel web structure immediately distinguishes it from orb weavers or cobweb spiders. The key is looking for that characteristic sheet web with funnel retreat rather than trying to identify the spider itself.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that most field guides focus on more common funnel weavers. Any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups, as it could represent an important range extension or population discovery.
compareHints: Distinguishing Coras juvenilis from its close relatives like Coras medicinalis or Coras montanus requires expert examination of reproductive structures and other microscopic features. In the field, focus on the funnel web structure and general behavior rather than trying to separate different Coras species, as they are nearly impossible to distinguish without laboratory analysis.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Distinguishing Coras medicinalis from its close relatives like Coras lamellosus or the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver requires examining fine details of body structure that are difficult to see in the field.
Distinguishing between different Coras species requires close examination of anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field.

The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver can be distinguished from its Coras relatives primarily by the male's distinctive leg spurs and its preference for higher elevation, cooler woodland habitats.
Coras aerialis is virtually indistinguishable in the field from its relatives like Coras medicinalis and Coras montanus without examining reproductive structures under magnification.
